questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: The Smallest Signal a Person Reports
questions.learningObjective: state what an absolute threshold measures and how it is estimated
questions.stem: An absolute threshold is estimated by presenting a faint stimulus on many trials and varying its strength until the person reports it about half the time. What does the resulting number describe?

options.text: The strength at which a signal of known physical size is detected half the time in an ideal observer with no costs of saying yes
The largest stimulus the person can detect without any strain, since the procedure looks for the point of comfortable seeing
options.misconception: describes a comfort criterion where the procedure sets a half-way point

options.text: The amount by which two equally strong stimuli must differ before the person notices the difference at all
options.misconception: names a difference threshold where the procedure presents a signal and a blank

options.text: The strength below which no signal exists in the physical world, so the figure bounds the stimulus rather than the person
options.misconception: treats a reporting threshold as a physical limit on whether the stimulus exists

questions.explanation: The phrase that does the work in this item is the last one, because a threshold is always a statement about an observer reporting a signal, not about the signal existing. A faint light is present on every trial whatever the person says, and what the procedure finds is the strength at which saying yes becomes more likely than saying no, which is why the conventional figure is the half-way point rather than the weakest stimulus ever glimpsed. The two conditions in the definition of an ideal observer are there because they matter: no cost attaches to a wrong yes and no benefit to a right one, so the figure describes perception rather than a person's caution. The comfortable-seeing option fails because that is a different and more practical quantity, and it is set by what feels easy rather than by what is detectable. The difference option fails because it describes a difference threshold rather than an absolute one. The physical-limit option fails because the same stimulus is presented on every trial and is never absent, so nothing in the procedure bears on whether it exists.
questions.hint: Ask what happens on the trials the person says they missed, and who is assumed to be reporting.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: The Proportional Rule for Brightness
questions.learningObjective: state Weber's law and the comparison it rests on
questions.stem: Weber's law says that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus is a fixed share of the stimulus rather than a fixed amount. What comparison does that claim rest on?

options.text: Two stimuli of different strengths differing by the same proportion, since the share is what is held constant
Two stimuli of the same strength differing by a fixed amount, since only then is a share meaningless
options.misconception: states the rival rule that a constant step gives, which is what the law denies

options.text: A single stimulus presented twice at different moments, since the law is about change over time
options.misconception: makes the law a claim about change across time rather than about a comparison

options.text: Two stimuli differing in kind rather than in strength, since the law concerns quality not quantity
options.misconception: extends the law to quality differences where a continuum of magnitude is required

questions.explanation: The law is a claim about proportionality, and the only way to state proportionality is as a comparison between two magnitudes, which is why the relevant comparison is between a baseline and that baseline plus a change. In practice the method is a two-alternative judgement in which a standard stimulus and a comparison stimulus are presented and the observer reports which is brighter, and the comparison that is varied is the ratio between them. The same-amount option fails because a fixed amount is precisely what the law denies, since if the detectable step were constant the ratio would fall as the baseline rose and the same step would become a smaller share of a larger stimulus. The time option fails because the law is about the discrimination between two simultaneous or closely successive stimuli and not about change across time, though a delayed comparison is a practical way of running it. The different-kind option fails because the law is about a continuum of magnitude, and applying it to quality is a different claim needing different evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what is held constant in the comparison that a fixed share implies.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Ratio Turned Into Two Thresholds
questions.learningObjective: apply Weber's law to predict a difference threshold at a new baseline
questions.stem: A brightness difference of 4 units is just detectable against a background of 20 units, so the proportional share is one fifth. Against a background of 250 units, what difference is just detectable?
questions.explanation: The proportional share is the detectable step divided by the baseline, so 4 over 20 is one fifth, and one fifth of 250 is 50. The size of the answer is the teaching point rather than the multiplication, because a brightness that has to be a quarter of the light in the room to be noticed is a very different perceptual situation from one where a twentieth is enough, even though the arithmetic is the same in both cases. Two qualifications belong with the figure. The share is not exactly constant across the whole range, since below an absolute threshold nothing is detectable at all and near the upper end the law is known to depart from the data, so the calculation is an estimate in the region where the law was measured. And the share depends on the observer, on the part of the retina being tested and on how the comparison is presented, so a different part of the eye will give a different answer for the same background.
questions.hint: Work out the share from the first pair, then multiply that share by the new background.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: What the Proportional Rule Assumes
questions.learningObjective: state the assumption built into a constant-ratio claim
questions.stem: A constant-ratio rule for brightness predicts that a detectable change always stays the same share of the background. What has to be assumed for the rule to hold across a range?

options.text: That the observer's sensitivity is in the range where a constant share was measured, and that it is not a claim about the whole scale
That a detectable change is a constant amount at every strength, since only then can the two rules be reconciled
options.misconception: offers the rival rule as though it were a way of saving the law

options.text: That the retina receives the same share of the light at every background, so the share itself is unchanging
options.misconception: assumes a constant retinal share, which is what the rule describes rather than assumes

options.text: That the eye adapts fully within a second, since adaptation is what would otherwise make the rule fail
options.misconception: asserts a fast adaptation time as the assumption behind a discrimination rule

questions.explanation: A proportional rule is a summary of a region rather than a law of the whole scale, and being clear about where it applies is the difference between using it and over-using it. The detectable step is not in fact a constant share everywhere: below the absolute threshold no step is detectable at any proportion, and at high intensities the share needed tends to change in a way the simple rule does not predict, which is one of the reasons an alternative that divides by the baseline plus the step is sometimes preferred. The honest statement is therefore that the share is approximately constant over the range in which it has been measured. The constant-amount option fails because it states the rival rule rather than reconciling anything, and if the step were constant the ratio would fall as the background rose. The unchanged-retina-share option fails because the proportion of light reaching the retina does change with intensity while the retinal gain compensates, and the compensation is what the rule is a description of rather than an assumption behind it. The adaptation option fails because placing full adaptation inside a single second is a claim about a different process, and the rule can be measured in conditions where adaptation is held steady.
questions.hint: Ask how far up and down the scale the share was actually measured, and what the rule says outside that region.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: One Trial in a Detection Task
questions.learningObjective: place a trial in a detection response matrix
questions.stem: A faint tone is presented and the observer presses a key saying it was there; the key is pressed 900 milliseconds after the tone began. Which cell of the response matrix does this trial belong to, assuming the tone was in fact presented?

options.text: A hit, since a signal was presented and the observer reported it, whatever the delay before the key press
A miss, since a signal was presented but the response came too late to count as a detection
options.misconception: treats a late report as though no report had been made at all

options.text: A false alarm, since a key press with no signal present is what a false alarm is
options.misconception: defines a false alarm for a trial the vignette says did carry a signal

options.text: A correct rejection, since the observer was given no way to know in advance whether a tone would sound
options.misconception: names the cell for a trial that did carry a signal and was reported

questions.explanation: The four cells of the matrix are defined by two facts, whether a signal was actually presented and whether the observer reported one, and a trial with both answers yes is a hit regardless of anything else about it. The delay in the vignette is the distractor, because a slow response changes the observer's apparent criterion rather than moving the trial to a different cell, and that is exactly why reaction time is collected alongside the response in this kind of study. The lack of advance knowledge is also not the point, since the observer is given no information about which trials carry a signal in a detection task, and that is the design rather than a defect. The miss option fails because a miss means the signal was presented and the observer did not report it, and a late report is still a report. The false-alarm option fails because no signal was in fact presented, which is the one thing the vignette states. The correct-rejection option fails for the same reason, and it additionally describes the opposite event.
questions.hint: Ask which two facts define each of the four cells, and then read only those facts off the trial.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Reading a Detection Table
questions.learningObjective: read hit and false-alarm rates out of a four-cell detection table
questions.stem: A detection study runs 40 signal trials and 40 blank trials. It records 30 hits, 10 misses, 12 false alarms and 28 correct rejections. Which set of rates is right?

options.text: A hit rate of 0.75 from 30 over 40 signal trials, and a false-alarm rate of 0.30 from 12 over 40 blank trials
A hit rate of 0.30 from 12 over 40, and a false-alarm rate of 0.75 from 30 over 40 blank trials
options.misconception: pairs each rate with the wrong kind of trial

options.text: A hit rate of 0.43 from 30 over 70 trials, and a false-alarm rate of 0.17 from 12 over 70 trials
options.misconception: divides both counts by the whole session instead of by each kind of trial

options.text: A hit rate of 0.75 from 30 over 40 and a false-alarm rate of 0.30 from 12 over 30, since only reported trials count
options.misconception: makes a false-alarm rate a proportion of reported signals rather than of blanks

questions.explanation: Each rate has its own denominator and the denominators are the two kinds of trial, not the whole session. A hit rate is hits over signal trials, so 30 out of 40 is 0.75, and a false-alarm rate is false alarms over blank trials, so 12 out of 40 is 0.30. It is worth noticing that a session has 80 trials but neither rate uses 80 as its denominator, because a hit and a false alarm cannot be counted against the same set of trials without the two rates becoming meaningless. The overall proportion correct would be 58 out of 80, which is a perfectly good figure to report and a poor basis for comparing observers, and that is the point of the table. The reversed option fails by pairing the two rates with the wrong trial types. The over-70 option fails by dividing by the total number of trials, which answers a question about the session rather than about either kind of trial. The over-30 option fails by counting a false alarm as a proportion of reported signals, which is a ratio between two different kinds of event and not a detection rate.
questions.hint: Ask which kind of trial each rate is a proportion of, since the two rates do not share a denominator.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Sensitivity Figure From Two Rates
questions.learningObjective: compute a sensitivity index from a hit rate and a false-alarm rate
questions.stem: An observer reports a signal on 90 percent of signal trials and also reports one on 10 percent of blank trials. The sensitivity index is the difference between the two rates in standard-score units. What is it?
questions.explanation: The two rates are converted to standard-score positions before they are subtracted, because a proportion alone is not a distance. A hit rate of 0.90 sits 1.28 standard deviations above the midpoint of a normal distribution and a false-alarm rate of 0.10 sits 1.28 below it, and the gap between those two positions is 2.56. Working in this way is what makes the figure comparable across studies, since it is no longer tied to the particular shapes of the two distributions and a different pair of rates can be compared with it directly. Two things are worth holding on to at the same time. The index here describes how well this observer separated signal from noise on this occasion, and a high value is compatible with a cautious observer or an eager one, since the rates being balanced is a separate matter from them being high. And the figure is a property of the observer and the noise, not of the signal, so it changes if the background noise is made harder.
questions.hint: Convert each rate to a standard-score position, then take the distance between the two positions.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Criterion and Sensitivity Held Apart
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a change of criterion from a change of sensitivity
questions.stem: After an observer is told that weak signals are common in the display, the hit rate rises and the false-alarm rate rises by about as much. What has changed?

options.text: The observer's criterion has moved, since the willingness to report shifted while the separation of signal from noise stayed as it was
The observer's sensitivity has improved, since more signals are now detected than before the instruction
options.misconception: reads a rise in detections as a gain in ability while the false alarms pass by

options.text: The signal has become stronger in the display, since both rates rose and a stronger signal would do that
options.misconception: believes a stronger signal would raise the false-alarm rate as well as the hit rate

options.text: The observer's eyesight has changed, since a change in the eye would raise both rates in the same direction
options.misconception: credits the eye for a pattern a moved reporting threshold produces on its own

questions.explanation: The pattern of movement is the diagnostic and it has to be read alongside what the two rates are computed over. Sensitivity is a distance between two distributions and it is fixed by the observer and the noise, so an instruction cannot change it: telling someone that weak signals are common does not make the signal easier to pick out of the background. A criterion is a threshold placed on that distance, and raising it produces more hits and more false alarms together, in roughly the fixed proportions that a constant distance implies. That is what the vignette describes. The improved-sensitivity option fails because it reads a rise in detections as a gain in ability, while the matching rise in false alarms is the signature of a moved threshold. The stronger-signal option fails because a stronger signal would raise the hit rate while leaving the false-alarm rate alone, since the false-alarm rate depends on the noise and the criterion rather than on the signal. The eyesight option fails because a change in the eye would change the distance and would not shift the two rates together in the way a moved criterion does.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two rates are computed over different kinds of trial, and what a change in the eye would do to each of them.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: One Observer at Three Instructions
questions.learningObjective: read a set of detection results as a criterion change rather than a sensitivity change
questions.stem: One observer completes the same detection task under three instructions. Neutral: 75 percent hits, 25 percent false alarms. Warned that weak signals are common: 93 percent hits, 55 percent false alarms. Warned that the display is faulty: 45 percent hits, 7 percent false alarms. What do the three rows show?

options.text: One sensitivity with three criteria, since the distance between the two rates is about 1.35 in all three and the rates move in opposite directions together
Three sensitivities with one criterion, since the hit rate ranges from 45 to 93 percent while the false-alarm rate falls with it
options.misconception: reads two rates moving in opposite directions as a change of ability

options.text: One criterion with three sensitivities, since the observer's accuracy is unchanged while the reporting threshold moves
options.misconception: puts the two quantities in the wrong order in the same pattern

options.text: One sensitivity with three criteria, since the overall proportion correct is 0.69 in the two warned conditions and 0.75 in the neutral one
options.misconception: makes a six-point consequence the substance and compares proportions over unlike trials

questions.explanation: Put the two rates of each row into standard-score positions and compare the distance. Neutral gives 0.674 above and 0.674 below, the warned-common row gives 1.475 and 0.126, and the warned-faulty row gives negative 0.126 and negative 1.475, and in all three cases the two positions are 1.35 apart. The sensitivity is therefore the same and only the midpoint between them has moved, which is exactly the picture of one observer with three thresholds for reporting. The overall proportion correct is the practical demonstration of the same point, since 69 percent in both warned rows against 75 percent in the neutral row, and a pair who had actually lost the ability to tell signal from noise would not have produced two different criteria with the same accuracy. The three-sensitivities option fails because the distance does not change and because a fall in the hit rate accompanied by a fall in the false-alarm rate is not what a loss of sensitivity produces. The one-criterion option fails on both counts in reverse. The last option fails because it reads a difference of six points as the substance when it is a consequence, and the proportions are computed over different trial types so they are not directly comparable in the first place.
questions.hint: Convert each row's two rates to standard-score positions and compare the distances, then compare the midpoints.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Why a Hit Rate on Its Own Is Ambiguous
questions.learningObjective: explain why an overall detection figure cannot be used to compare observers
questions.stem: Two observers take the same detection task. One gets 58 correct out of 80 and the other 62, so the second is called the better detector. What is wrong with that comparison?

options.text: The figure mixes two kinds of trial, so it rises both when an observer is more sensitive and when one simply reports more often
The figure is too small a sample to report at all, since a difference of four trials cannot be shown to be real
options.misconception: blames sample size for a figure that is misleading whatever the sample is

options.text: The figure is invalid because the two observers were not given the same number of signal trials to begin with
options.misconception: invents an imbalance in trial types that the vignette does not report

options.text: The figure is valid but useless, since detection accuracy carries no information about an observer's sensitivity
options.misconception: dismisses the figure as empty rather than as the wrong quantity for the task

questions.explanation: The single figure is the proportion of trials answered correctly across both signal and blank trials, and both ways of being a poor detector produce the same total. An observer who cannot separate signal from noise at all and reports yes to everything gets 50 percent, because half of the signal trials are right and half of the blank trials are wrong, and so does an observer who never reports anything. A cautious observer on a sensitive task and an eager observer on the same task can produce the same total while having very different capacities, which is the entire reason for separating the two rates before comparing observers. The two rates are not a refinement of a good measure; they are the measure. The small-sample option fails because sample size is a real concern for any figure but it is not what makes this one misleading, since a large sample would make the misleading comparison more confident rather than less. The unequal-trials option fails because the vignette gives the same task to both, and a correction for unequal trials would not address the ambiguity anyway. The useless option fails because the figure is not devoid of information, it is simply not the quantity a comparison requires.
questions.hint: Ask what an observer who always says yes and one who always says no would each score, and what that says about the figure.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: The Sequence Inside One Detection Trial
questions.learningObjective: sequence the operations in a detection decision
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order in which the events of a single trial in a detection task occur.

options.text: A signal or a blank is presented, chosen according to a schedule the observer does not know
A background of noise is present throughout, and the signal is set at a fixed level above it
The observer forms some impression of whether something is there, based on the noise and the signal together
That impression is compared with the observer's threshold for reporting, which need not be a fixed number
The observer responds, and the accuracy and the time of the response are both recorded

questions.explanation: The order is a sequence of dependencies, and the reason the noise comes second is worth stating rather than treating it as a detail. The signal level is described as a fixed level above the noise, and that phrase only means something once the noise is specified, since the same signal is easy to detect in quiet and hard to detect in loud, and it is this relationship rather than the absolute strength that determines the difficulty of the task. The observer's impression then follows, since an impression about presence is formed from the combined evidence, and the comparison with a threshold comes after the impression exists because a threshold is something the impression is measured against rather than something that produces it. The response is last and it is recorded together with its time because the two together are what the study uses to separate a change of threshold from a change in the capacity, since a faster response to the same accuracy is a different situation from a slower one at the same accuracy. The order that puts the threshold before the impression fails because a threshold is a comparison point and a comparison needs two things, and the order that puts the response before the comparison fails because the observer's decision is the comparison.
questions.hint: Start with what is presented and against what background, then what the observer forms, then what it is measured against, and finally the response.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Two Kinds of Threshold
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an absolute from a difference threshold
questions.stem: One threshold is the faintest tone a person can detect in silence. Another is the smallest change in tone a person can detect against a tone already playing. What distinguishes them?

options.text: The first asks whether any signal is present against nothing, and the second asks whether one signal differs from another
The first is measured with two tones and the second with one, so the procedures differ in how many stimuli appear
options.misconception: counts stimuli rather than asking what the observer is comparing

options.text: The first is a property of the ear and the second a property of the listener's memory for the first tone
options.misconception: moves the second threshold into memory rather than into a simultaneous comparison

options.text: The first stays the same over a session and the second changes as the listener adapts to the tone already playing
options.misconception: asserts opposite stability for the two thresholds without any basis in the case

questions.explanation: The two thresholds ask different questions and the answers are used for different purposes. An absolute threshold is a detection question, and the stimulus that is too faint to detect is a real stimulus that simply is not picked out of the background, which is why the procedure presents a signal and a blank on separate trials. A difference threshold is a discrimination question, since a signal is already audible and the observer has to say whether it is the same or different, and this is why the presentation is a pair of tones rather than a tone and a silence. The distinction matters in practice because the two quantities behave differently across the range, so a discrimination that is easy at a moderate baseline becomes much harder at a low one even though nothing has changed about the listener. The procedures option fails because a detection task also involves two kinds of trial, and it is the presence or absence of a signal rather than the number of stimuli that makes it a detection task. The memory option fails because the second threshold is measured against a signal being heard, not against a remembered one. The stability option fails because both thresholds are re-measured across a session and adaptation affects both of them.
questions.hint: Ask what the observer is being asked to compare in each case, and whether anything is present in the background.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: What Constant Light Stops Signalling
questions.learningObjective: state what sensory adaptation is a response to
questions.stem: A faint sound that was obvious on the first second fades from awareness while it continues unchanged. What has happened, and what does it tell us?

options.text: Sensitivity to an unchanging signal has declined, so a constant signal stops carrying information about anything
The signal itself has weakened, since a receptor that fires as much as before would still be detected
options.misconception: attributes a change in response to a change in the stimulus the premise rules out

options.text: The listener has forgotten the sound, so what is lost is a memory rather than a sensitivity
options.misconception: explains a fade that reverses on a change as though it were a loss of memory

options.text: The sound has moved to another pitch, so it is still present but is no longer at the frequency it started at
options.misconception: recasts a decline in sensitivity as a change in the frequency of the sound

questions.explanation: The useful way to put adaptation is in terms of what it is for, and a signal that does not change carries no news, so the system reduces its response to it and reserves capacity for what does change. The fading is therefore not a loss in the physical signal, which is a fixed property of the sound being played, but a change in the response of a system tuned to changes. That is also why the effect is strongest for a constant signal and weak for one that fluctuates, and why a signal becomes visible again the moment it changes. The weakened-signal option fails because the premise of the vignette is that the sound continues unchanged, and a receptor's response cannot alter the physical stimulus. The memory option fails because nothing in the vignette involves remembering a sound, and a fade that reverses the instant the sound changes is not a forgetting curve. The pitch option fails because pitch is not what is reported to change, and a change of pitch would be a change in the signal rather than a decline in sensitivity to it.
questions.hint: Ask what an unchanging signal tells an observer that a changing one does not, and what a fade that reverses on a change would indicate.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Brief Flash Under a Brief Mask
questions.learningObjective: interpret a stimulus presented below the threshold and masked
questions.stem: On some trials a picture is shown for twenty milliseconds, and on others it is followed twenty milliseconds later by a random pattern that lasts two hundred milliseconds. On the masked trials observers are later asked to choose between a left and a right arrow, and they do no better than chance. What does this show?

options.text: That the design can raise a question about effects below threshold but cannot settle one, since choosing between options needs a comparison the task does not supply
That no processing of the picture occurred at all, since any processing would have beaten the chance level in this task
options.misconception: treats a task that cannot register an effect as proof that none occurred

options.text: That the mask destroyed a picture that would otherwise have been seen, since twenty milliseconds is long enough to see clearly
options.misconception: treats a short exposure as inadequate when the mask is the new element

options.text: That the observers were guessing correctly half the time, which is exactly the rate a two-alternative task produces by definition
options.misconception: reads the chance rate itself as a positive finding about guessing

questions.explanation: The result is uninformative in a way that is easy to misread, and the reason lies in what a two-alternative judgement requires. To do better than chance the observer has to pick the arrow that was there, and doing that requires a memory of which side the picture was on that survives the mask, so the task cannot distinguish no processing from processing that left no usable trace. A stimulus presented below the absolute threshold is in any case not visible, and the claim that a sub-threshold stimulus can nonetheless influence a judgement is a claim about measurable effects rather than about seeing, and it has to be tested with a measure that does not itself demand a conscious comparison. The no-processing option fails because a task that is incapable of detecting an effect cannot show that none occurred. The destroy option fails because twenty milliseconds of a simple picture preceded by a longer blank is ordinarily enough to see, and it is the mask that is new, not the exposure. The by-definition option fails on the arithmetic, since a two-alternative task produces 50 percent by guessing and this result is exactly that, which is the point rather than a positive finding.
questions.hint: Ask what a person would have to do in order to beat chance here, and whether the task lets them do it.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Rare Condition in a Large Group
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of flagged cases that are real when the condition is rare
questions.stem: A screening test is used on 1,000 people in whom the condition affects 1 percent. The test detects 90 percent of those who have it and gives a positive result to 10 percent of those who do not. What share of positive results are real?

options.text: About 8 percent, since of 1,000 people 10 have the condition, 9 are detected and 99 are wrongly flagged
About 50 percent, since 90 percent detected out of 100 percent flagged splits the positives evenly
options.misconception: applies a rate about the affected group to the set of positives

options.text: About 90 percent, since that is the share of affected people the test finds, so it must be the share of positives that are real
options.misconception: reads a figure about the affected group as a share of the flagged group

options.text: About 82 percent, since 90 percent of positives being right leaves 10 percent wrong and the remainder must be right
options.misconception: subtracts one rate from another and calls the remainder a share of positives

questions.explanation: The shares have to be converted to counts before anything can be compared, and that is the whole exercise. One percent of 1,000 is 10 people with the condition, of whom 90 percent, which is 9, are detected. The other 990 do not have it and 10 percent of those, which is 99, are wrongly flagged. The positives are therefore 9 real ones among 108, and 9 over 108 is a little over 8 percent. The pattern is the standard one for a test that is good at detecting and poor at rejecting when the condition is rare, and it is why a screening result of this kind is a reason for further examination rather than a diagnosis. The even-split option fails because it treats the detection rate as though it applied to the positive results. The 90-percent option fails by reading a figure about the affected group as though it were about the positive group. The 82-percent option fails because it subtracts one rate from another and calls the remainder a share of positives.
questions.hint: Convert each rate to a number of people, add the positives, and then take the share that are real.

questions.stem: In 1,000 people the condition affects 1 percent, the test finds 90 percent of those who have it and flags 10 percent of those who do not. First work out how many positives there are in total, then the share of them that are real.

100 positives, of which about 9 percent are real, since 1 percent of 1,000 is 10 and 90 percent of 10 is 9
options.misconception: leaves the wrongly flagged cases out of the positive total

options.text: 108 positives, of which about 90 percent are real, since the test finds 90 percent of the affected group
options.misconception: reports a rate about the affected group as the share of positives that are real

options.text: 99 positives, of which about 8 percent are real, since the wrongly flagged cases are the only ones counted
options.misconception: counts only the false positives and then divides by a total that excludes the real ones

questions.explanation: The two steps have to be done in that order because the share of positives is meaningless until the number of positives exists. Ten people have the condition and 9 of them are found, while 990 do not and 99 of them are wrongly flagged, so the positives come to 108. The share that are real is then 9 over 108, which is 8.3 percent, and it is worth saying why the figure is so low even though the test performs respectably. The test is doing exactly what its rates say, and the low share comes entirely from the base rate, since 990 people without the condition are producing ten times as many false positives as the condition produces real ones. A positive result from a test like this is therefore a reason to look further, and a test that flagged fewer of the healthy would raise the share without any change in how good the test is at finding the condition. questions.hint: Find the real positives and the false ones separately, add them, then divide the real ones by that total.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: What a Below-Threshold Claim Has to Show
questions.learningObjective: state the evidential requirement for a claim about stimulus processing without awareness
questions.stem: A claim that a stimulus too weak to be seen can still affect a later judgement has been made many times. What must such a claim show to be more than a lucky guess?

options.text: A measured change in behaviour or physiology, tested against a chance baseline that the design itself can produce
That observers can later report the stimulus accurately when asked directly whether they saw it
options.misconception: asks for the acknowledgement the claim is about, which would abandon it

options.text: That the stimulus was above the absolute threshold for at least some of the people in the sample
options.misconception: requires the stimulus to be visible, which removes the claim rather than testing it

options.text: That the effect appears in a single highly suggestible participant whose report is later confirmed by the experimenter
options.misconception: treats one confirmed report as sufficient when the confirmation is not independent

questions.explanation: The measurement problem is that a stimulus below threshold cannot be acknowledged by the people who received it, so the only available evidence is some effect they did not have to intend, and the design has to make that effect impossible to produce by chance. A two-alternative choice does not meet the requirement, since choosing requires a usable memory of the stimulus and a person who can choose has by definition registered something. A behavioural or physiological measure is the appropriate kind of evidence, and it has to be measured against a baseline the design produces rather than against a figure from another study, because the rate of a lucky guess depends on the number of alternatives and on how the options are arranged. The self-report option fails because it asks for the acknowledgement the claim is about, and a person who can report the stimulus is not the population the claim concerns. The above-threshold option fails by abandoning the claim. The single-participant option fails because one confirmed report is a coincidence until it is replicated, and the experimenter's confirmation is not independent of the suggestion.
questions.hint: Ask what the person who received the stimulus could possibly report, and what a design has to measure instead.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Claims About Thresholds and Detection
questions.learningObjective: judge which claims about thresholds and detection are supported
questions.stem: Four claims about thresholds and detection are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: A threshold is a property of an observer detecting a signal rather than a property the signal either has or lacks
Two observers with the same overall detection accuracy can differ in both their sensitivity and the threshold they report at
A constant proportional step can be assumed across the whole range of a stimulus, since the share is a property of the sense organ
options.misconception: extends a regional rule to the whole scale and overlooks the region with no threshold at all

options.text: Raising an observer's threshold for reporting makes them more accurate, since fewer signals are missed at a higher threshold
options.misconception: reverses the effect of a higher threshold on the miss rate and calls it an accuracy gain

questions.explanation: The first supported claim is the foundation the rest of this area rests on, since the signal is physically present on every trial whether or not it is picked out, and what a threshold describes is the observer's performance on a particular procedure with a particular criterion. questions.hint: Ask what a threshold is a fact about, and how a single accuracy figure could hide two different observers.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: What the Retina Hands On
questions.learningObjective: state what the retinal image contributes to an experience of seeing
questions.stem: Light entering the eye forms an image on the retina that is upside down and out of focus. What follows for what a person actually sees?

options.text: The retinal image is a signal rather than the experience, since what a person sees is built from it rather than read off it
The person sees an upside-down blur, since the image on the retina is the whole of what is seen
options.misconception: identifies the retinal signal with the experience it is supposed to produce

options.text: The brain must correct the image before the signal is formed, since a signal cannot arrive upside down
options.misconception: puts the correction upstream of transduction rather than after it

options.text: The blur shows the retina is not working properly, since a sharp image is what the retina should produce
options.misconception: treats ordinary optical blur as a fault in the retina

The corrects-first option fails on timing, since correction is a matter of interpreting a signal that has already been formed. The faulty-retina option fails because a soft image is what the optical system produces over a range of viewing distances, and a retina that only accepted sharp images would be useless.

questions.learningObjective: compare the specialisations of the two retinal receptor types
questions.stem: Two receptor types in the retina differ sharply in what they do well. Which pairing of specialisations is correct?

options.misconception: splits colour and brightness into two receptors as though they were independent

options.misconception: assigns the types to functions and leaves nothing to receive the light

options.misconception: treats a difference in density as though it were a clean partition of the retina

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Reading a Dark Adaptation Curve
questions.learningObjective: interpret the two phases of a dark adaptation curve
questions.stem: A plot shows the smallest light a person can detect while sitting in the dark. The curve drops steeply for about seven minutes, flattens, then falls again slowly for a further twenty. What does the second fall show?

The first receptor type growing steadily more sensitive, since a second phase cannot begin without one

options.text: The eye having finished adapting at seven minutes, with the later fall being a fault in the measurement
options.misconception: treats the informative second phase of the curve as an artefact

options.misconception: assigns the second phase to colour, which the curve does not measure

The colour option fails because the curve tracks the smallest detectable light and says nothing about which channel is carrying it.

questions.learningObjective: explain a contrast effect in terms of interactions between neighbouring regions
questions.stem: A wide grey band carries a narrow band of a very similar grey that looks distinctly darker, while the same narrow band on a lighter background looks lighter. What is going on?

The two bands fall on different parts of the retina, since a display's brightness varies from one side to the other
options.misconception: invites a retinal difference that a flat display does not produce

options.text: The narrow band is physically darker in the first position, since a display cannot hold its output constant
options.misconception: explains a processing effect by a change in the light the display sends

options.misconception: requires a comparison between positions where the surround alone does the work

The comparison option fails because the second band looks lighter on its own account, with the darker surround present, and no comparison between the two positions is required.
questions.hint: Ask what is held constant in the display, and therefore where the difference must come from.

questions.learningObjective: compute the angle subtended by a stimulus at two viewing distances
questions.stem: A letter five tenths of a millimetre tall is read at 5 metres, which puts it at about 0.34 minutes of an angle. First work out the angle at 2 metres, then say how many times larger that is.

options.text: About 0.86 minutes of an angle, which is two and a half times the angle at 5 metres
About 0.17 minutes of an angle, which is a half of the angle at 5 metres
options.misconception: scales the angle up when the distance falls instead of down

options.text: About 0.86 minutes of an angle, which is twice the angle at 5 metres
options.misconception: gets the angle right and takes the change in distance for the ratio of distances

options.misconception: turns a distance falling to two fifths into a fivefold increase in angle

questions.learningObjective: explain why a missing patch of retina does not appear as a dark patch
questions.stem: A person reports that a small patch of background seems to vanish where an object is about to be, and reports no dark spot in the field of view at all. How can that be?

options.text: The image falls on a part of the retina that cannot tell colours apart, and the person sees a grey patch instead

The grey-patch option fails by confusing the absence of receptors with the presence of a receptor type that lacks one kind of colour channel. The no-such-spot option fails because a person is not a good witness to the presence of a gap they cannot see, which is the whole point.

questions.learningObjective: explain why mixing lights and mixing pigments give different results
questions.stem: A red light mixed with a green light gives a yellow that looks like light, while red and green paints mixed together give a muddy brown. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: Lights add, so the mixture keeps sending both kinds of wavelength, while pigments subtract, so the mixture removes more light than either alone

options.misconception: offers brightness as the mechanism where the direction of light differs

The impurity option fails because dullness on mixing is general to subtractive mixing and does not require any particular pigment to be faulty. The ranking option fails because the difference is in the mechanism by which a mixture is formed, not in how strong a colour is considered to be.

questions.stem: A red book on a desk looks red in daylight and under a lamp, even though the light reaching the eye differs in both cases. What is being held constant?

options.text: The relationship between the wavelengths reflected from the page and the light falling on it, so a ratio rather than a level is reported
The level of light reaching the eye, so the perceived colour is a function of brightness alone
options.misconception: makes colour a function of brightness where a ratio between two changes is what matters

options.text: The wavelengths of the light source, so the book reflects a fixed set whatever is shining on it
options.misconception: holds the illuminant steady and lets the page's reflectance vary instead

options.text: The observer's memory of the book's colour, so a familiar object keeps the colour it was last seen to be
options.misconception: makes the constancy an effect of memory rather than of the current ratio

questions.explanation: Two things change when the illumination changes and neither of them is the page. The light arriving at the eye changes in level and in the balance of wavelengths reaching it, and what the page sends back changes in proportion, so the relationship between the two is much more stable than either is on its own. Reporting that relationship rather than either quantity is what lets an object keep its name across a change of light, and it is a case where the perceptual system is doing something that a reading of the signal alone would not deliver. It is also bounded: a change of illuminant that alters which wavelengths the page reflects in the first place does change the colour, so the constancy holds within a range and not universally. The brightness option fails because brightness changes considerably in the case while the colour does not. The illuminant option fails because the light source plainly does not keep its wavelengths. The memory option fails because the constancy is complete for unfamiliar objects as soon as they are lit differently.
questions.hint: Ask what changes at the eye, what changes at the page, and what stays in proportion between them.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Why Opponent Channels Appeal and What They Leave Open
questions.learningObjective: evaluate what an opponent-channel account explains and what it leaves open
questions.stem: Accounts built on opponent channels are widely used to explain why some colour mixtures cancel. Explain what they account for, and what they leave unsettled.

answer.exemplar: The account gets something right that a purely additive account cannot, and it is worth being exact about what. Two lights that differ in brightness and yet look identical to a particular observer cannot be described by a system that only adds light, because adding cannot make two totals coincide when one is larger, whereas a comparison along a dimension with a cancelling value can make them coincide exactly. That is the sense in which a comparison is needed, and it is the reason opponent arrangements were proposed. What the account leaves unsettled is substantial, and two items matter more than the rest. The first is the number of axes: a three-axis arrangement fits the cancellation data well, and further opponent effects have been reported since, so the fitted scheme has been revised without the original data being discredited, which is a normal feature of an account being developed rather than a failure. The second is where the comparison happens, since opponent effects can be produced in the retina, which shows the comparison may begin early and does not show that it completes there, and a retinal finding neither establishes nor rules out a cortical stage. A third difficulty is that the account organises the phenomena it was built from, so the fit is good by construction and the real tests are predictions it was not designed to make, such as how a mixture behaves when one component falls below the absolute threshold, or what happens when the two components are presented to different parts of the retina. On present evidence the account earns its place as a workable description of what the data show and has not been shown to be the mechanism itself.

questions.explanation: The answer has to state the cancellation problem that a comparison solves, identify the number of axes and the place of the comparison as the two open questions, and note that a good fit to the data the account was built from is not by itself a test of it. It should propose a prediction the account was not designed to make as a way of distinguishing the possibilities.
questions.hint: Ask what two lights of different brightness can do that addition alone would not allow, and what the account was not designed to predict.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Table of Sound Intensities
questions.learningObjective: read a logarithmic intensity scale rather than a linear one
questions.stem: Sound levels are reported in decibels against a reference intensity of a trillionth of a watt per square metre. Which set of values is right?

options.text: An intensity of 0.01 gives about 100 decibels, 0.02 about 103 and 0.04 about 106, since doubling adds about three
An intensity of 0.01 gives about 10 decibels, 0.02 about 20 and 0.04 about 40, since the scale is linear in intensity
options.misconception: treats a logarithmic scale as though it were proportional to intensity

options.text: An intensity of 0.01 gives about 100 decibels, 0.02 about 200 and 0.04 about 400, since the scale repeats the intensity
options.misconception: multiplies the reading by the intensity instead of adding a constant to it

options.text: An intensity of 0.01 gives about 1 decibel, 0.02 about 2 and 0.04 about 4, since the reference is the unit of the scale
options.misconception: drops the reference intensity the reading has to be measured against

questions.explanation: The decibel is a logarithmic scale, and the reason it exists is that intensities people can encounter differ by many orders of magnitude, so a scale that treated them proportionally would put almost everything in the bottom of its range. What the scale does is take the ratio of the intensity to the reference and then multiply the logarithm of that ratio by ten, and the consequence worth remembering is that equal steps on the scale mean equal ratios of intensity. Doubling is a step of about three decibels, which is why the three rows in the correct option are three apart rather than doubling, and it is why a change of twenty decibels means a hundredfold increase rather than a twofold one. That last figure is the one that gets quoted most often and it is regularly mishandled. The linear option fails because it treats the scale as though it were proportional to intensity. The repeating option fails by multiplying the reading by the intensity instead of adding a constant to it. The unit option fails because it drops the reference the reading is measured against, without which the number means nothing.
questions.hint: Work out the ratio of each intensity to the reference, then remember that a doubling is about three decibels.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Intensity Against Loudness
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a measured physical ratio from a perceived magnitude
questions.stem: One sound is measured as ten times as intense as another, and listeners usually judge the louder one to be considerably more than ten times as loud. What does the gap show?

options.text: The decibel scale measures a physical ratio and loudness is a perceptual magnitude, so the two are related without being the same quantity
The decibel scale is wrong, since a tenfold rise in intensity ought to sound like a tenfold rise in loudness
options.misconception: demands a proportional match between a physical ratio and a perceived magnitude

options.text: The ear responds in proportion to intensity everywhere, so any mismatch must have come from careless listening
options.misconception: blames the listeners for a systematic feature of the scale

options.text: Loudness and intensity are two names for the same thing, and the gap only reflects how carefully each was measured
options.misconception: collapses two quantities and so explains nothing by the difference between them

questions.explanation: Intensity is what the measurement gives: a physical quantity with an objective value that two instruments will agree about. Loudness is what the listener reports, and it is a perceptual magnitude, which means it is what the scale already calls a decibel value on the basis of equal-loudness matches rather than equal intensities. The two therefore track one another closely enough to be useful and not so closely that one can be substituted for the other, and the case in the vignette is the standard demonstration that a ratio of intensities is not a ratio of experiences. The wrong-scale option fails by assuming that a physical scale ought to deliver a proportional perceptual scale, which would only be true if the ear responded like a physical instrument. The blame option fails because the mismatch is systematic and shared by listeners, which is a fact about hearing rather than about the people. The same-thing option fails because it explains nothing: a difference between two quantities cannot be a difference in how carefully they were measured if the quantities are identical.
questions.hint: Ask what the instrument measures and what the listener reports, and whether one can stand in for the other.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Hearing One Band of Pitches
questions.learningObjective: localise a hearing difficulty to a frequency range
questions.stem: After an illness a person reports that most sounds are heard clearly but that one band of pitches has become hard to distinguish, so that voices are hard to tell apart. What does the pattern suggest?

options.text: A limited region of the frequency map in the inner ear is affected, since damage there would hit one band rather than all sound
The whole auditory system has lost sensitivity, since every sound now arrives at the same strength
options.misconception: extends a restricted difficulty into a general loss across all of hearing

options.text: The person's memory for sounds has failed, since a difficulty of discrimination is a failure of memory
options.misconception: reinterprets a difficulty while the sound sounds as though it were a recall failure

options.text: The outer ear is at fault, since it funnels sound and a fault there would remove all frequencies alike
options.misconception: puts the fault where it would spare no band of frequencies

questions.explanation: The diagnostic feature is the restriction, and a system that maps frequency onto place can fail in one place without failing everywhere. The inner ear is arranged so that different regions respond to different ranges of frequency, and a person who can hear clearly across most of the range while finding one band hard to sort out is describing a loss confined to part of that map, which is the pattern a localised damage would produce. It is also why a person's complaint tends to be about voices rather than about sound in general, since much of what intelligibility depends on is the fine structure in a restricted band. The general-loss option fails because it discards the reported restriction, and a general loss would make everything hard. The memory option fails because the difficulty is present while the sound is sounding, not in recalling it afterwards. The outer-ear option fails because the outer ear does not sort by frequency in the way described, and a fault there would not spare a band.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the hearing system is arranged so that one place handles one range of frequencies.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Two-Hertz Change in Pitch
questions.learningObjective: express a frequency change as a percentage and as a cycle duration
questions.stem: A tone at 440 cycles a second is raised to 442. First work out the size of the change as a percentage of the original, then the duration of one cycle of the original tone in milliseconds.

options.text: About 0.45 percent, and about 2.27 milliseconds for one cycle of the original tone
About 2 percent, and about 4.54 milliseconds for one cycle of the original tone
options.misconception: divides by the new frequency and then doubles the period

options.text: About 0.45 percent, and about 4.54 milliseconds for one cycle of the original tone
options.misconception: has the percentage right and the reciprocal of the frequency wrong

options.text: About 4.5 percent, and about 0.45 milliseconds for one cycle of the original tone
options.misconception: attaches the two results to the wrong questions and gets both wrong

questions.explanation: The two steps use the number in different ways and it is worth being clear which. The change is two cycles out of 440, so as a percentage of the original it is two over 440, which is 0.0045, or 0.45 percent, and using 442 as the base would give a fractionally different and less natural figure. The duration of one cycle is the reciprocal of the frequency, so a thousand milliseconds divided by 440 is 2.27 milliseconds, and this is the number that makes the scale concrete: at 440 cycles a second the waveform repeats about two and a quarter thousand times a second, so a rise of two cycles a second is a very small change and is heard as a slight sharpening rather than as a new note. An octave is a doubling and a thousand cycles a second is the conventional reference for the top of a keyboard instrument, which is the other figure worth having alongside these. The two-percent option divides by the wrong base and then doubles the period. The halved-period option has the percentage right and the reciprocal wrong. The reversed option has the two results attached to the wrong questions.
questions.hint: Take the change over the original for the percentage, and a thousand divided by the frequency for the cycle duration.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: The Sense That Reports Gravity and Head Movement
questions.learningObjective: identify the vestibular sense and what makes it unusual
questions.stem: A sense in the inner ear reports head position and the pull of gravity and contributes to knowing where the body is and how it is moving. What is it, and what is its distinctive feature?

options.text: The vestibular sense, whose receptors lie in the semicircular canals and the balance organs and which is unusual for reporting the body's own motion
The kinesthetic sense, whose receptors lie in the joints and which is the main source of information about gravity
options.misconception: assigns the inner ear's job to receptors in the joints

options.text: The olfactory sense, whose receptors respond to head position and which is therefore involved in balance
options.misconception: assigns balance detection to receptors that respond to chemicals

options.text: The cutaneous sense, whose receptors in the skin of the feet supply the primary signal about head position
options.misconception: makes the skin of the feet the primary source of information about head position

questions.explanation: Three things make this sense stand out among the others and each of them is worth naming. Its receptors are in the inner ear and are mechanically operated, since the fluid and the membranes inside the canals move with the head and that movement is what is detected. It reports the body's own motion rather than something in the environment, which makes it a sense of a moving observer, and no other sense does that job. And it is involved in more than balance, since it contributes to the sense of self in space, and a person who has lost it reports difficulty both in staying upright and in trusting where they are. The kinesthetic option fails by assigning the inner ear's job to the joints, which report position and movement of the body rather than its orientation against gravity. The olfactory option fails outright, since receptors for smell respond to chemicals. The cutaneous option fails because receptors in the feet do contribute to balance and to orientation, but they are not the primary signal about head position and the case describes the inner ear.
questions.hint: Ask which sense reports the observer's own motion rather than something in the environment, and where its receptors sit.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: The Number of Basic Tastes
questions.learningObjective: treat the list of basic tastes as a claim that has been revised
questions.stem: It is often stated that there are five basic tastes. How should that claim be handled?

options.text: As a claim whose number has been revised upward as further receptors were identified, so a list of five is a dated figure rather than a settled one
As a settled fact, since the five were established by experiment and have not been questioned since
options.misconception: presents a working assumption as a final one that later work revised

options.text: As a claim about the tongue, since each of the five is said to be carried by a different part of it
options.misconception: revives a regional map of the tongue that was withdrawn as unsupported

options.text: As a claim about smell, since most of what is called taste is actually odour arriving from the nose
options.misconception: substitutes a different question about odour for one about primary tastes

questions.explanation: This is one of the items in the field most often taught in a form that has aged badly, and the honest treatment is to say what the claim is and what has happened to it. There was a period during which a short list of primary tastes was taught as a fact, and a diagram assigning each to a region of the tongue was taught alongside it; the diagram was withdrawn when it was shown to be unsupported, since receptors for the different primary tastes are distributed across the tongue rather than partitioned. The list itself was later extended when receptors for further candidates were identified, so a figure of five survives as a historical number and a current one is larger. The right habit in an item like this is to treat the list as something the evidence can change. The settled option fails because it presents a working assumption as a final one. The tongue option fails by reviving the withdrawn regional map. The smell option fails by substituting a different question, since most of what is called taste does involve smell, and that says nothing about how many primary tastes there are.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to this list as further receptors were identified, and what happened to the diagram that went with it.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: From Light to a Reported Object
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages by which light becomes a reported object
questions.stem: Put these five stages in the order in which light is turned into an object a person reports seeing.

options.text: Receptor cells in the retina respond in patches, and each patch reduces the response of the neighbours around it
The signals travel along the optic nerve to the visual areas of the brain at the back of the head
Light is brought to a focus on the retina and converted by receptor cells into electrical signals
Cells in the visual areas respond differently to different features of the image, including its orientation
Those responses are combined with what is already known, and the combination is what the person reports seeing

questions.explanation: The order is a chain in which each stage is impossible before the one before it, and two of the steps are worth explaining rather than merely listing. The focusing and transduction come first, since they are the only stage at which light itself is involved and everything after it is already a signal. The interactions between neighbouring patches come next and not later, because they happen within the retina itself, and putting them after the nerve would place a retinal process inside the brain, which is the direction of the error this step invites. The nerve and the visual areas follow, and the feature-responsive cells come after the signal has arrived, since a cell cannot respond to the orientation of something it has not been given. The last step is the one that makes a person report an object rather than an array of responses, and it is placed last because it is a combination of what has arrived with what was already in the system. The order that puts the interactions after the nerve option fails because it relocates a retinal process. The order that puts the feature cells before the signal arrives fails because it inverts the direction of travel. The order that adds knowledge before the signal has left the retina fails because it puts interpretation upstream of the data.
questions.hint: Start where light itself is involved, keep everything that happens inside the retina together, then follow the signal into the brain and out to the report.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Estimating a Threshold in a Two-Alternative Task
questions.learningObjective: design a procedure for estimating a difference threshold with a two-alternative judgement
questions.stem: A laboratory wants to measure the smallest brightness difference most observers can detect, using a two-alternative judgement rather than a yes-and-no report. Design a procedure and say what it has to report.

answer.exemplar: Present a standard and a comparison stimulus and ask which is brighter, then adjust the comparison until the observer's answers stop favouring it, using a two-step or staircase procedure so that the figure reported is an average over reversals rather than the last setting tried. Present the pair in one order on half the trials and the other order on the rest, since a constant order lets a preference for one position pass for a sensitivity to the difference and that is the standard control for it. Hold the duration, the background, the retinal location and the distance constant across trials, because a difference threshold measured at one part of the retina at one duration is a statement about those conditions and not about the eye in general. Record the proportion of trials on which the standard was judged brighter and compare it with the 50 percent a two-alternative judgement produces when the two are indistinguishable, since that comparison is what gives the estimate its meaning. Report the estimate together with the step size and the number of reversals used, and report how many observers fell within a stated distance of the median, because a threshold is a population statement and a single observer's value is not one. Say in advance how the reversals will be summarised, since a point on a psychometric curve needs a convention and different conventions give different numbers from the same data.

questions.explanation: The design has to establish where the observer's answers stop favouring one stimulus, which is a different quantity from the point at which a yes-and-no report changes, and the two-alternative procedure is chosen precisely because it does not require a report about whether anything was seen. A single adjustment is not enough, since it finds only the last setting tried, and the order of the pair has to be varied or a position preference will be reported as a difference threshold. Reporting the proportion correct against chance, the step size and the number of reversals is what makes the figure comparable with another laboratory's, and a threshold quoted on its own cannot be evaluated at all.
questions.hint: Ask where the observer's answers change rather than where a report changes, and what would let a position preference masquerade as a threshold.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Grouping Rules as Defaults
questions.learningObjective: state the status of a perceptual grouping principle
questions.stem: A set of principles holds that elements close together, similar in appearance or following a smooth path are read as belonging together. What is the status of such principles?

options.text: They describe what a display tends to be read as, so a display arranged against them is the case that tests them
They describe a rule the visual system always obeys, so an arrangement that violates it cannot be seen at all
options.misconception: makes the principles exceptionless and so puts them beyond the reach of a test

options.text: They describe how a display was made, since designers choose these groupings so that figures stay legible
options.misconception: attributes the grouping to the designer rather than to the observer

options.text: They describe a stage that comes before any light reaches the eye, so no stimulus could contradict them
options.misconception: places the grouping upstream of the stimulus that any test would have to present

questions.explanation: The interesting use of a grouping principle is as a statement about a default rather than a law, and the distinction shows up in the displays that are deliberately built against them. A row of dots is read as a line because of proximity, and a version in which the dots are grouped instead by similarity or by a common path will be read the other way, and the version read the other way is not unseeable, it is simply seen differently. That is what makes a principle testable. The always-obeyed option fails because a principle that admits no exception is one that can never be put at risk, and the displays above are read in spite of it rather than failing to be read. The designed option fails because the effect is in the observer, and a designer who arranged the display differently would only change which default was available to be adopted. The before-the-light option fails by placing the grouping upstream of the stimulus, and a grouping principle is a claim about the reading of a stimulus, so it cannot be settled without one.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a display built deliberately against one of the principles.

questions.learningObjective: separate the sense of taste from the contribution of smell to flavour
questions.stem: After a head injury a patient says food has almost no flavour, though textures and temperatures still give pleasure. What does the pattern suggest?

That the sense of taste is gone, since flavour and taste are one experience under a different name
options.misconception: collapses flavour and taste into a single experience that cannot be partly lost

The appetite option fails because a change in appetite is a change in motivation and would not spare the sense of taste for the basic tastes. questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Figure, Ground and Completion
questions.learningObjective: explain what a display with an outline and no middle shows and does not show
questions.stem: A display shows a shape whose middle is left out, so only its outline is drawn, and viewers see a solid shape. Explain what that shows and what it does not show.

answer.exemplar: The display establishes that a solid surface is experienced where the display contains only an outline, and that the experience is not a faint or doubtful version of a surface. Viewers do not report an empty middle with a boundary around it; they report a shape, which tells us that the missing region is not passed on as a gap in the percept. That is the content of the finding, and it is a bounded claim about the relationship between a display and a report. What it does not establish is how the missing part is supplied, and several quite different mechanisms would do the job: a system that fills in the region enclosed by a closed outline because the alternative readings are implausible, a system that reports the shape its recent experience predicts, and a system that treats a closed contour as an edge of an object because closed contours are what objects in the world usually make. A display that closes a contour in one place and leaves it open in another is the kind of test that tells them apart, and so is one in which a region that was completed turns out to have been something else. The demonstration also says nothing about the signal reaching the retina, since the retinal image contains an outline and not a surface, so the work is being done after transduction, and the demonstration cannot say where after. The wider significance is the one that matters for the rest of the topic: what a person reports seeing is not a transcript of the signal, and a gap in the signal need not appear as a gap in the experience.

questions.explanation: The answer has to say what the display establishes about the relationship between signal and report, list mechanisms that could produce the completion, and propose a display that would separate them. It should note that the retinal signal contains an outline rather than a surface, so nothing here locates the work in time or place.
questions.hint: Ask what the display literally contains, and what a viewer would report if the region were being passed on as a gap.

questions.stem: A sheet of paper looks white under an ordinary lamp and still looks white when the room is lit by a dimmer lamp of a different colour. What must be held for that to happen?

options.text: The relationship between the light arriving at the eye and the light leaving the surface, so a ratio is reported rather than an amount
The amount of light arriving at the eye, so perceived lightness follows the level of illumination directly
options.misconception: makes perceived lightness track the level of illumination, which the case shows it does not

options.text: The colour of the lamp, so a change of lamp has to be matched by a change in what the paper looks like
options.misconception: predicts that any change of illuminant changes the appearance, which the case denies

options.text: The observer's expectations about lamps, so an unusual illuminant makes the paper look wrong until it is reinterpreted
options.misconception: makes the constancy depend on familiarity with lamps rather than on the current light

questions.explanation: Changing the lamp changes both the level of light arriving at the eye and the balance of wavelengths in it, and the paper's apparent lightness survives both changes, so neither of the two can be what is being reported. What is comparatively stable is the relationship between the illuminant and the share of it the surface sends back, and reporting that relationship rather than either quantity is what allows a surface to keep its name. The effect is bounded and the bound is worth knowing: it holds while the illuminant stays within a range over which the surface reflects a recognisable set of wavelengths, and a strongly coloured light inside a room makes white objects look coloured, which is the failure the account predicts. The amount option fails because the amount changes and the lightness does not. The lamp-colour option fails because it predicts exactly that failure and the case reports the opposite. The expectations option fails because the constancy is complete for unfamiliar objects, and a person seeing a new surface for the first time under the new lamp still sees it as the same lightness as before.
questions.hint: Ask which two quantities change when the lamp changes, and which of them the perception does not follow.
