questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Wall in Sun and in Shade
questions.learningObjective: reason about a change in reflectance between two photographs
questions.stem: The same wall is photographed in bright sun and in shade, and in the shade photograph it looks lighter even though the photographer matched the overall brightness of the two images. What is the wall's reflectance doing?

options.text: Returning a different share of the light in each case, and the wall is seen as one object because that share is not what is reported
Returning the same share in each case, so the whole difference between the photographs comes from the light falling on it
options.misconception: treats reflectance as an absolute brightness rather than as a share of the illuminant

options.text: Returning more light in the sun, since a sunlit surface always reflects a larger fraction of what reaches it
options.misconception: assumes the share a surface returns depends on how strong the illuminant is

options.text: Returning less light in the sun, since the brightness of the light a surface returns depends on the surface alone
options.misconception: holds that the returned light depends on the surface alone and ignores the illuminant

questions.explanation: Matching the overall brightness of two images does not make them carry the same information, and that is the trap. If the shutter and aperture are set so that a sunlit wall and a shaded wall record the same overall level, the difference between the two records lies in how that level was arrived at, and a wall seen through a full patch of direct sun and the same wall in shade are not in that position with respect to the light by any means alike. The reflectance of the surface is a property of the surface, and it is a share of whatever arrives, which is why the sunlit version returns a smaller share of a much larger amount. The same-share option fails because it treats reflectance as an absolute brightness, which is the conflation the constancy is usually used to expose. The more-in-sun option fails because a surface's share does not depend on how strong the illuminant is. The surface-alone option fails for the same reason in the other direction, since how much light leaves a surface depends on what fell on it as well as on the surface.
questions.hint: Ask whether matching overall brightness makes the two photographs carry the same information about the surface.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Two Distances, One Apparent Size
questions.learningObjective: compute the size that keeps a given apparent size at a new distance
questions.stem: A 6 cm coin held at 2 metres is reported to look the same size as a coin held at 6 metres. First work out the viewing distance the second coin is at, then its size.

options.text: A viewing distance of 6 metres, and a coin of 2 cm, since the same apparent size needs the same size-to-distance ratio
A viewing distance of 3 metres, and a coin of 3 cm, since halving the distance halves the apparent size
options.misconception: halves the distance and the size together, which leaves the ratio unchanged

options.text: A viewing distance of 6 metres, and a coin of 6 cm, since the coin itself is not the thing that changed
options.misconception: holds the size fixed and so leaves the ratio unchanged as well

options.text: A viewing distance of 2 metres, and a coin of 2 cm, since only the size of the coin may be allowed to vary
options.misconception: reports a size change at the same distance, which enlarges the retinal image

questions.explanation: Apparent size is governed by the size of an object relative to its distance, and a size that looks the same at three times the distance has to be a third as big, which gives 2 cm at 6 metres. The reason the item is worth doing is that the retinal image is not what is being matched. A 6 cm coin at 2 metres and a 2 cm coin at 6 metres produce retinal images of exactly the same size, so on a retinocentric account they ought to look identical for the uninteresting reason that the signals match, and the case is where the retinocentric account and the constancy part company. The point of the demonstration is that people adjust size to distance rather than going with the retinal match, and an object twice the retinal size at a further distance is not reported as twice as big. The halving option fails by halving the distance and the size together, which leaves the ratio unchanged and so changes nothing. The unchanged-size option fails because it holds the ratio constant rather than varying it, so it cannot produce a change in apparent size. The same-distance option fails because the two coins would then be different sizes in the image, and a difference in the image is not what a size constancy removes.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be held constant for two objects to look the same size, and what that says about the retinal image of the pair.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: The Construction Claim At Its Strongest
questions.learningObjective: state the strongest defensible form of the claim that perception constructs
questions.stem: A claim often made about perception is that the visual system does not read off a faithful copy of what lands on the retina but builds an interpretation. What is the strongest form of this claim?

options.text: That the signal underdetermines the scene, so more than one scene fits it and the system has to choose among the candidates
That the visual system is unreliable, since an interpretation cannot be as good as the image on the retina
options.misconception: turns a claim about information into a claim about accuracy

options.text: That the retina is redundant, since everything it sends is already available from the movements of the eyes
options.misconception: makes the retinal signal unnecessary to the percept

options.text: That perception is mostly memory, since almost all of what is seen is drawn from what has been seen before
options.misconception: substitutes a claim about prior knowledge for a claim about underdetermination

questions.explanation: The defensible core of the claim is about information and not about accuracy or effort, and it is worth stating it in that form because the weaker versions are easy to dismiss. A signal arriving at the retina is compatible with more than one arrangement of surfaces and lights, and the fact that it is compatible with several is a fact about the signal rather than about the system that receives it. Choosing among the candidates requires something beyond the signal, and that is what the claim asserts. The unreliable option fails because underdetermination is not error, and a system that picks the right candidate out of several is doing something other than guessing. The redundant-retina option fails because the signal and the eye movements do not carry the same information, and it turns a claim about what the signal fails to specify into a claim that the signal is unnecessary. The mostly-memory option fails because a reliance on prior knowledge is a different claim from a claim about underdetermination, and the case of a display that is seen differently when the expectation is changed is a case about prior knowledge rather than about ambiguity in the signal.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about error, about information, or about what the signal does not specify.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: An Ecological Reply to the Construction Claim
questions.learningObjective: assess what an argument from successful action establishes and what it leaves open
questions.stem: A reply to the construction claim argues that ordinary action succeeds far too often for perception to be a free interpretation. Explain what that reply establishes and what it does not.

answer.exemplar: The reply takes its force from the fact that people act on scenes and are usually right, and a reply built on a record like that is not easily waved away. A person crossing a road in poor light, reaching for a cup without looking, or stepping over an obstacle is correct far more often than chance would allow, and if a perception were a free construction of whatever happened to fit the cues, that success would be a coincidence repeated without end. So the reply establishes something real: the interpretation is not unconstrained, the signal carries information that bears on what is out there, and a demonstration that one display is underdetermined is a statement about what the signal fails to specify rather than a statement that nothing constrains it. What the reply does not establish is the conclusion it is often taken to support, which is that the construction claim is simply false. An account of perception can allow a large amount of interpretation and still be constrained enough to guide action, and the reply says nothing about how much interpretation takes place, only that some information survives. Nor does it dispose of any particular demonstration, since a demonstration that one cue influences a judgement is entirely compatible with a system that uses cues accurately across the rest of the field. The test that would help is one that measures the size of the interpretive freedom in a task where the outcome can be checked, because a system constrained by the need to succeed should show little freedom there, and a free-construction account predicts more of it than that allows.

questions.explanation: The answer has to grant the force of the point that guided action is usually successful, then say why that constrains the construction claim without refuting it, and propose a test that measures how much interpretive freedom there is where success can be checked.
questions.hint: Ask how often guided action succeeds, and what a demonstration of underdetermination does and does not say about constraint.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Threshold Beside a Construction
questions.learningObjective: synthesise what a threshold result and a figure-ground result jointly establish
questions.stem: A faint grating is detected in 50 percent of trials, and separately a display that can be read as a square or as a set of strips is seen as a square by most viewers. Synthesise what these two findings do and do not establish between them.

answer.exemplar: The two results answer different questions and the useful synthesis resists pressing them into one claim. The threshold result is about the point at which a signal begins to be picked out at all: below it the evidence is not sufficient for a report, which is a statement about a signal, an observer and a procedure, and it is bounded by both the particular grid used and the half-way convention used to define the point. The figure-and-ground result is about a signal that is comfortably above any threshold being organised one way rather than another: the same pattern supports two readings and one of them is adopted, which is a statement about what an adequate signal does not specify. Taken together they describe a system that is constrained at one end and underdetermined at the other, and that combination is coherent rather than paradoxical, because the room to interpret grows with the amount of evidence, so a bare faint grid leaves almost nothing to choose between and a well-formed drawing leaves a great deal. What the pair does not establish is a single account joining the two, and it is worth saying that a threshold account on its own has nothing to say about how an adequate signal is organised, so it cannot explain the second result even though it is consistent with it. The study that would connect them varies the richness of a display while finding the threshold for each and asks whether the range of readings available to a viewer grows as the display moves further above threshold; a construction account predicts that it does and an account built only on additive sensitivity does not.

questions.explanation: The answer has to keep the two results apart by the question each answers, note that together they describe a system constrained at one end and underdetermined at the other, and propose a study that varies display richness against threshold in order to connect them.
questions.hint: Ask what each result is a statement about, and what a threshold account alone has to say about the second of them.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Two Fins, One Line
questions.learningObjective: interpret a length judgement displaced by a pictorial depth cue
questions.stem: Two equal lines are drawn, each with arrowheads at its ends. On one the fins point outward and it looks longer; on the other they point inward and it looks shorter. What does the pair show?

options.text: A pictorial depth cue supplied by the fins changes the perceived length, which is what happens when a size cue is misapplied
The outward-finned line really is longer, since adding marks to a line can change the length of the line
options.misconception: explains a perceptual effect by a change in the drawn line itself

options.text: One of the two viewers is mistaken, since the lines are the same length and cannot look different
options.misconception: rejects a shared perceptual report as though it were an error

options.text: The fins themselves are perceived, since the effect is caused by the marks being added rather than by their arrangement
options.misconception: credits the marks rather than their arrangement, which is what differs between the two

questions.explanation: The fins are a pictorial cue in the sense that a scene drawn with them is intended to be read as a scene, so the outward version suggests a line nearer the observer and the inward version a line further away. The size constancy that normally corrects for distance does the wrong thing here, because the correction is calibrated for real depth cues that arrive with the geometry of an actual scene, and a drawing supplies a suggestion of depth with nothing behind it, so the correction displaces a length judgement that was correct to begin with. That is the whole of the demonstration, and it is a demonstration about a mechanism rather than about the accuracy of vision. The line-is-longer option fails by making the drawn length depend on the marks added to it. The mistaken-observer option fails because two people seeing the same display report the same displacement, and treating a shared report as an error explains nothing. The marks option fails because the fins are identical in the two versions and only their arrangement differs, so the marks themselves cannot be the cause.
questions.hint: Ask what the fins suggest about depth, and what a constancy calibrated for real scenes then does to a length judgement.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Why an Illusion Is Not a Failure
questions.learningObjective: explain the status of a disputed illusion without settling it
questions.stem: People report that the moon looks much larger when it is low in the sky than when it is high, and the accounts of why this happens do not agree. Explain what the disagreement is about and what any account must handle.

answer.exemplar: The disagreement is about which information the judgement of apparent size is using, and the accounts are genuinely competing rather than one being a refinement of another. One proposes that the moon is compared against objects near the horizon, which in haze look small, so that the moon must be large; another proposes that the moon's own image is distorted as it sits lower and that the eye accommodates to it differently; a third proposes that what the moon is compared against is the afterimage left by the bright sky the observer has just been looking at. The status of the demonstration is what the item really turns on. What a person who reports the difference has established is a difference in experience, and that is a finding whatever the account of it turns out to be, and a report of apparent size is not something the observer could have got wrong by misdescribing a physical measurement. Any account has to handle at least three things: why the size is judged larger when the moon is low; why the effect weakens when the horizon is hidden behind a building, since that removes whatever the moon was being compared against; and why brightness does not account for it, since a bright light low in the sky looks hazier and smaller rather than larger, so a brightness-based story predicts the opposite of what is reported. What the reports do not establish is which account is right, and the honest summary is that a misjudgement in a specific direction is established while its cause is not.

questions.explanation: The answer has to set out the competing accounts without picking one, list the observations any account must handle including the horizon-occlusion control and the failure of a brightness story, and separate what the reports establish from what they leave open.
questions.hint: Ask what else could be near the moon to compare it with, and what happens to the effect when the horizon is hidden.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Mixing Two Lights in a Fixed Ratio
questions.learningObjective: express a fixed mixing ratio as a pair of shares
questions.stem: Two lights are mixed in the ratio 3 to 1, the brighter being the one given the larger share. First work out the share of the mixture made up by the brighter light, then the dimmer one.

options.text: Three quarters of the mixture is the brighter light, and a quarter is the dimmer one
Three fifths of the mixture is the brighter light, and two fifths is the dimmer one
options.misconception: treats a ratio of three to one as though it had five parts

options.text: Three quarters of the mixture is the brighter light, and three quarters is the dimmer one as well
options.misconception: gives both lights the same share and so describes a different mixture

options.text: A third of the mixture is the brighter light, and two thirds is the dimmer one
options.misconception: assigns the smaller share to the light the ratio gives the larger one

questions.explanation: A ratio of 3 to 1 describes four equal parts, and the shares follow from adding them up rather than from anything about the ratio itself, so three of the four parts belong to the brighter light and one to the dimmer. That is 0.75 and 0.25, and the two must sum to one, which is the quickest check available. The reason the item is in a unit on perception rather than on arithmetic is the connection to the additive property of light: a mixture of lights keeps sending both sets of wavelengths, so the proportions in the mixture are proportions of the light arriving at the eye, and a mixture can be made to match a single light of a third colour by choosing the right proportion, which is the observation that made a comparison-based account of colour necessary. The two-fifths option treats the ratio as five parts rather than four, which is the standard slip when a ratio is expressed as though the two numbers were percentages. The two-thirds option gives both lights the same share and so describes a different mixture entirely. The reversed option assigns the smaller share to the brighter light, which is the opposite of the ratio as given.
questions.hint: Add the two parts of the ratio together to get the whole, then take each part as a share of that whole.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Two Lines That Should Look Equal
questions.learningObjective: identify the cue exploited by a converging-lines display
questions.stem: Two equal lines are drawn across a pair of converging lines, as on a track receding away. The line nearer the top of the picture is judged the longer. What is being exploited?

options.text: A size cue that is valid in a real scene and misleading here, since the converging lines imply a difference in distance
A difference in the length of the two lines, since a drawing of this kind must have been drawn inaccurately
options.misconception: explains the judgement by an inaccuracy that would spoil the demonstration

options.text: A difference in sharpness between the two lines, since a clearer line is judged to be the longer one
options.misconception: attributes the judgement to sharpness, which the construction holds constant

options.text: A difference in contrast against the background, since contrast is what determines perceived length
options.misconception: attributes the judgement to contrast rather than to the implied difference in distance

questions.explanation: The converging lines are a depth cue and the display works by supplying one that the size constancy will act on. In a real scene two equal bars at different distances do have different lengths, and a system that compensates for distance will judge the further one as the larger; here the depth is only implied, and the two lines are equal, so the compensation displaces a judgement that was correct. What the display demonstrates is a mechanism operating in a case where it should not, which is a bounded and rather instructive result. The inaccurate-drawing option fails because the whole point of the arrangement is that the two lines are equal, and an inaccuracy would spoil the demonstration rather than explain it. The sharpness option fails because nothing in the construction makes one line clearer than the other, and clarity is not a length cue in this sense. The contrast option fails for the same reason, since both lines are drawn the same way against the same background, and contrast plays no part in the judgement the display produces.
questions.hint: Ask what the converging lines suggest, and what a compensation for that suggestion does to two lines that are actually equal.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: What a Perceptual Demonstration Is Evidence About
questions.learningObjective: state the scope of a claim established by a perceptual demonstration
questions.stem: A display produces a misjudgement and the arrangement responsible for it is known. What has been established by showing the two together?

options.text: That a particular cue contributes to the judgement, which is a claim about how one display is read rather than about seeing in general
That the visual system makes errors in general, since a single misjudgement is enough to show the system is unreliable
options.misconception: generalises from one display to a verdict on the whole system

options.text: That the cue causes the misjudgement, since producing the display is the same as producing the cause
options.misconception: confuses establishing sufficiency with identifying a cause

options.text: That the visual system could not do without the cue, since a cue that is sometimes misleading is still required
options.misconception: reads a demonstration of use as a demonstration of necessity

questions.explanation: A demonstration of this kind is a strong piece of evidence and its strength lies in the control, since showing the arrangement and then showing the misjudgement disappear when the arrangement is changed is a much better case than either alone. What it establishes is a claim about a cue's contribution to a judgement in a specified display, and the parts of the claim that can be defended are the parts that name the display and the judgement. The errors-in-general option fails because the systematic quality of the result is a virtue for a demonstration and not a licence for a verdict on the whole system, and much of what the system does is compensation rather than error. The cause option fails because producing a display establishes sufficiency, since the misjudgement follows from the arrangement, and sufficiency is not the same as identifying a cause, which would require ruling out what else might be doing the work. The required option fails by reading a demonstration of use as a demonstration of necessity, and a cue can be influential without being indispensable.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison between the two displays rules out, and what kind of claim a sufficiency demonstration supports.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: An Illusion Beside a Threshold
questions.learningObjective: synthesise what an illusion result and a threshold result jointly establish
questions.stem: One display both displaces a length judgement and has a detection threshold for a faint grid, and both measures come from the same observers. Synthesise what the pair of results does and does not establish.

answer.exemplar: The pair is worth setting side by side because it is easy to let one result stand in for the other, and they belong to different levels of the same system. The illusion result concerns how an adequate signal is read: the lines are the same length, the arrangement is known to matter, and the judgement is displaced in a predictable direction, so the result identifies a cue contributing to a length judgement under those conditions and says how to remove the displacement. The threshold result concerns how little signal is needed before any report is possible, so it identifies the point at which the evidence runs out for a grid, and it is bounded by the particular grid used and by the convention used to define the point. Neither is a statement about the accuracy of perception in general, and a single summary calling perception either reliable or unreliable would be the wrong conclusion to draw from them. What the pair does show is that a system with a clear threshold can be systematically displaced above it, so the two findings are not competing and neither is evidence against the other. What the pair does not show is that the same observers are displaced on both measures, which is a specific question and the natural next study, since a person can be a cautious detector and an uncritical length judge at the same time. Nor does it show that the two measures draw on the same processing, since the displays and the judgements differ in nearly every respect, and pooling them into one report about the observers would be a mistake.

questions.explanation: The answer has to place the two results at different levels of the same system, refuse a general verdict on the accuracy of perception, and identify what the pair does not establish about the relation between the two measures in the same observers.
questions.hint: Ask what each result is a statement about, and whether either one speaks to the other.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: The Steps of a Staircase Estimate
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a staircase threshold estimate
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order in which a staircase estimate of a threshold is obtained.

options.text: The procedure starts at a level already shown to be detected about half the time, so that it begins near the point of interest
A stimulus is presented and the observer reports whether it was present
A detection turns the level down and a miss turns it up, by one step or by a fixed multiple of the level
This continues until the levels at which the answer changes have been sampled several times over
The average of those change points is reported, together with the step size and the number of changes

questions.explanation: The order is a chain of dependencies, and the first step is the one most often left out in summaries because it sounds like a preliminary. A staircase works by nudging a level up and down around the point where the observer's answers change, so if it starts far from that point it spends most of its trials getting there and finishes with a figure that describes a starting level rather than a threshold. Starting near the point of interest means the later reversals are all of the relevant kind. Presentation and report come next, the adjustment rule follows the report because the rule is applied to what came back, and the repetition comes after the adjustments have begun because reversals only accumulate once the level is oscillating around the right place. The report is last, and it has to carry the step size and the number of reversals because those two quantities set the resolution and the reliability of the average, and a figure quoted without them is a number with no error attached to it. The order that presents a stimulus before a starting level is set fails because there is nothing to adjust from. The order that reverses the adjustment rule fails because the level would run away from the point rather than towards it. The order that reports before the reversals have accumulated fails because an average needs a set of points to average.
questions.hint: Start where the procedure is already close to the point of interest, then follow what happens on each trial and when the figure can be written up.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Separating a Criterion From Sensitivity
questions.learningObjective: design a comparison of two groups that can separate criterion from sensitivity
questions.stem: A laboratory has two groups of observers and wants to know whether they differ in sensitivity or in willingness to report. Design a study that could settle it.

answer.exemplar: Run the same detection task on both groups with the same instructions in the same words, in the same room, with the same practice and the same number of trials, so that whatever differs between them is what was selected rather than what happened on the day. Vary the signal level across its whole range instead of fixing it at one value, since a single level cannot separate a moved threshold from a changed distance, and a change in level moves the apparent distance in a way that has to be estimated rather than assumed. Analyse each group from the pair of rates at every level, not from the overall proportion, because the overall proportion is produced by sensitivity and threshold together. The test is then direct: if the two groups differ in sensitivity, the two distributions are further apart in one group and their midpoints sit in the same place, whereas if they differ only in willingness to report, the distance is the same and the midpoint moves. Report the distance and the midpoint for each group at each level rather than a single figure, since the whole argument rests on the two being separable. Report how many participants were run in each group and how many were excluded before the results were seen, because groups chosen for a property of the eye or of the head are groups in which the two are correlated in an uncontrolled way, and say in advance that a difference in the midpoint alone would count as a result rather than as a failure to find a difference.

questions.explanation: The design has to compare the groups on the pair of rates at several signal levels rather than on an overall proportion, and it has to hold instructions, practice and setting constant, since a single signal level cannot separate the two quantities. A difference in sensitivity shows as a larger distance between the rates and a difference in willingness as a moved midpoint, and reporting the two separately is what makes the conclusion possible. Excluding participants after seeing the results is the other thing that has to be declared, because a group chosen for a property of the eye is a group in which willingness may also differ.
